analysis.one_liner: Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.
analysis.headline: The House passed the SAVE Act 221-198 on July 10, 2024, but the Senate never voted and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAVE Act would have required everyone registering to vote in a federal election to show documentary proof of citizenship — a passport, a REAL ID that indicates citizenship, a birth certificate meeting seven specific conditions, or a similar document. People who registered by mail or online would have had to bring those documents in person to an election office before they could be registered. States would have had to run ongoing programs to find and remove noncitizens from the rolls, and election officials who registered someone without proof could have been sued or criminally charged. The House passed it on a nearly party-line vote, but the Senate never brought it up.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had become law, the clearest gainers would have been political: the bill gave House Republicans a roll-call vote on an election-integrity theme 12 weeks before the 2024 election [S7, S9]. Citizens who want citizenship verified before registration would have gotten mandatory document checks and ongoing state programs to find and remove noncitizens from the rolls [S2]. States would have received citizenship data from federal agencies within 24 hours of asking, with no fee [S5].

how_it_helps.text: Barred states from processing any federal voter registration unless the applicant presents documentary proof of citizenship: a REAL ID indicating citizenship, a valid U.S. passport, a military ID with a service record, a government photo ID showing U.S. place of birth, or an ID paired with a certified birth certificate or naturalization papers [S2, S5].

Required every state to run an ongoing program to identify noncitizens on the rolls using federal databases, and to remove them; federal agencies had to answer state verification requests within 24 hours and could not charge a fee [S5].

Provided a fallback for applicants who lack the standard documents: they could sign an attestation under penalty of perjury and submit other evidence for a state or local official to review, with a uniform affidavit the official had to sign [S5].
Added enforcement aimed at officials: a private right of action against an election official who registers an applicant without documentary proof, plus criminal penalties for doing so [S2, S5].

analysis.who_pays: Eligible citizens who do not have a passport, a driver's license that indicates citizenship, or a birth certificate that matches their current legal name would have faced new hurdles to register — and mail and online registration could no longer be completed without an in-person trip to an election office [S5]. State and local election offices would have shouldered new citizenship-verification programs, exposure to private lawsuits, and criminal penalties for registering an applicant without proof [S2, S5].
analysis.who_pays_short: Citizens lacking passports or matching documents

drawbacks.text: The qualifying-document list is narrow. A standard driver's license only works if it indicates citizenship or is paired with a certified birth certificate meeting seven conditions, and the list does not include marriage licenses or court name-change orders — so a voter whose birth certificate bears a name different from their current ID could have had no qualifying document even with the birth certificate in hand [S5].

Applicants who used the federal mail registration form could not be registered until they presented documents in person to an election office by their state's registration deadline — ending fully by-mail registration for people who cannot easily travel, though states were told to make reasonable accommodations for voters with disabilities [S5].

Election officials who registered an applicant without documentary proof could have been sued by private citizens and faced criminal penalties, a legal risk that could have pushed local offices to reject eligible applicants rather than chance a lawsuit [S2, S5].

The bill would have taken effect immediately upon enactment, with the Election Assistance Commission given only 10 days to adopt and transmit implementation guidance to state election officials [S2, S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose — keeping noncitizens off federal voter rolls — targets conduct that is already a federal crime under existing law, so its practical effect would have been to add a document requirement to every registration. The burden would have fallen on eligible citizens: those without passports, whose licenses do not indicate citizenship, or whose birth certificates no longer match their legal names. The enforcement teeth — private lawsuits and criminal charges against election officials — risked turning routine registration into a legal hazard for the people who run it. Supporters' strongest argument was public confidence in election rolls; the fallback attestation process offered some relief but left the decision to individual officials under threat of liability. On balance, the costs to eligible voters and election offices outweighed the added protection, though the question is contested — and none of these effects took effect because the bill never became law.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a nearly party-line vote in July 2024, but Senate leadership never scheduled it, and it sat on the Senate calendar until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Chip Roy introduced the bill on May 7, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration [S1, S7].
The committee reported the bill as amended by a 6-1 vote on June 14, 2024, and it was placed on the House calendar [S7].
On July 9, 2024, the Rules Committee reported H. Res. 1341, which allowed floor debate but barred amendments — a closed rule [S7].
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill to committee failed 184-197, with all 184 yes votes from Democrats and all 197 no votes from Republicans [S8].
The House passed the bill 221-198 on July 10, 2024: 216 of 220 voting Republicans in favor, and 5 of 213 voting Democrats in favor [S9].
The Senate received the bill, read it twice, and placed it on the General Orders calendar on July 23, 2024; no further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Eligible voters who lack passports or whose documents do not match their current names kept the simpler registration system, and election officials avoided new lawsuit and criminal exposure. Republican campaigns gained a recorded vote to campaign on even though the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voters without passports; campaigns with a talking point

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost perfectly by party — 216 of 220 voting Republicans in favor against 198 of 213 voting Democrats opposed, with only 5 Democrats crossing over [S9]; the motion to recommit was 184-197 along the same lines [S8].

industries.note: The bill produced a party-line roll-call vote 12 weeks before the 2024 election, giving its supporters a campaign record, and tighter rolls with challenge tools shift electoral risk toward one side. Its gain runs through political advantage rather than through any benefit delivered to voters.

The bill would have required these offices to verify citizenship documents, run ongoing noncitizen-identification programs, and face private lawsuits and criminal penalties for registering an applicant without proof. Their interest in avoiding that liability ran alongside voters' interest in easier registration.
